title: R for Longitudinal Data Analysis
text:
Preface
This Quarto book contains materials to accompany the two-day short course, R for Longitudinal Data Analysis run by Liam Wright of the Centre for Longitudinal Studies (CLS) at University College London. Comments and questions about this book can be submitted to the GitHub repository.
To follow along, you will need to have R and RStudio installed on your computer and to possess data from the National Child Development Study (1958 British Birth Cohort) and the Millennium Cohort Study, downloaded from the UK Data Service .dta (Stata) format and arranged into directory structures following the instructions here here and here.
The following R packages are used on the course.

title: 6  Interlude: Data Cleaning
text:
6.1 NCDS
The following chapters cover analysis and require cleaned data. Here we will prepare two datasets (one for MCS, one for NCDS) allowing us to assess the association between childhood/adolescent cognitive ability and body mass index (BMI). These datasets will include BMI at each sweep in which it is measured, as well multiple measures of cognitive ability and a set of control variables (age of BMI measurement, sex, mother’s and father’s education, mother and father’s BMI, and ethnicity). More detail on the various cognitive measures are described in Moulton et al.’s (2024) excellent report on the measurement of cognition in the British birth cohorts.
The code below uses the functions that we have seen in previous chapters. Some small mistakes are left in, as in the next chapter we see functionality for checking that data conforms to expectations. The code is not fully commented as yet, but will be annotated further in due course.
The packages we will use are:
We also define some “helpers” that will be used to clean both the NCDS and MCS data.
ncds_raw <- list()
ncds_clean <- list()

load_ncds <- function(file, vars = c()){
  glue("{ncds_fld}/{file}") %>%
    read_dta(col_select = c(matches("NCDSID|ncdsid"),
                            all_of(vars)))
}

## a. Sample, Sex and Ethnicity ----
ncds_raw$xwave <- load_ncds("xwave/ncds_response.dta",
                            c("n622", "ethnicid"))

ncds_clean$xwave <- ncds_raw$xwave %>%
  mutate(
    sex = negative_to_na(n622) %>% as_factor(),
    ethnic_group = case_when(
      ethnicid == 1 ~ "White",
      ethnicid %in% 2:6 ~ "Non-White"
    ) %>%
      factor(c("White", "Non-White"))
  ) %>%
  select(ncdsid, sex, ethnic_group)

## b. Parental Characteristics and Cohort Member Cognitive Ability ----
ncds_raw$sweep_0y_16y <- load_ncds("0y-16y/ncds0123.dta",
                                   c("n914", "n2928", "n2396", "n2397",
                                     "n1196", "n1199", "n1202", "n1205"))

lookup_ncds_parent_edu <- c(7:13, 15, 17, 19) 

ncds_clean$sweep_0y_16y <- ncds_raw$sweep_0y_16y %>%
  mutate(
    across(where(is.labelled), negative_to_na),
    
    father_edu_years = lookup_ncds_parent_edu[n2396],
    mother_edu_years = lookup_ncds_parent_edu[n2397],
    
    father_weight_kg = n1196 * 0.5 * 6.35029, # Increments 1/2 stone units
    father_height_m = n1199 * 2.54 / 100, # In inches
    father_bmi = father_weight_kg / (father_height_m^2),
    mother_weight_kg = n1202 * 0.5 * 6.35029,
    mother_height_m = n1199 * 2.54 / 100,
    mother_bmi = mother_weight_kg / (mother_height_m^2),
    
    verbal_11 = as.double(n914),
    vocab_16 = as.double(n2928),
  ) %>%
  select(ncdsid, father_edu_years:vocab_16,
         -matches("_(height_m|weight_kg)$"))

## c. Cohort Member BMI ----
ncds_raw$anthropometrics <- tribble(
  ~file, ~vars,
  "0y-16y/ncds0123.dta", c("dvht07", "dvht11", "dvht16", "dvwt07", "dvwt11", "dvwt16"),
  "23y/ncds4.dta", c("dvwt23", "dvht23"),
  "33y/ncds5cmi.dta", c("n504731", "n504734"),
  "42y/ncds6.dta", c("htmetre2", "htcms2", "htfeet2", "htinche2", 
                     "wtkilos2", "wtstone2", "wtpound2"),
  "42y-44y Biomedical/ncds42-4_biomedical_eul.dta", c("htres", "wtres"),
  "50y/ncds_2008_followup.dta", c("DVHT50", "DVWT50"),
  "55y/ncds_2013_derived.dta", c("ND9HGHTM", "ND9WGHTK"),
) %$% # magrittr 'exposition' pipe - allows you to extract columns within pipe
  map2(file, vars, 
       ~ load_ncds(.x, .y) %>%
         rename_with(str_to_lower)) %>%
  reduce(~ full_join(.x, .y, by = "ncdsid"))

ncds_clean$anthropometrics <- ncds_raw$anthropometrics %>%
  rename_with(~ str_replace(.x, "^dvht", "height_") %>%
                str_replace("^dvwt", "weight_")) %>%
  rename(height_55 = nd9hghtm,
         weight_55 = nd9wghtk) %>%
  mutate(
    across(where(is.labelled), negative_to_na),
    
    height_33 = values_to_na(n504731, 0) / 100,
    weight_33 = n504734,
    
    height_42 = case_when(
      between(htmetre2, 1, 2) & between(htcms2, 0, 100) ~ htmetre2 + (htcms2 / 100),
      between(htfeet2, 3, 8) & between(htinche2, 0, 11) ~ ((htfeet2 * 12) + htinche2) * 2.54 / 100
    ),
    weight_42 = case_when(
      !is.na(wtkilos2) ~ wtkilos2,
      between(wtstone2, 5, 31) & between(wtpound2, 0, 15) ~ ((wtstone2 * 16) + wtpound2) * 0.453592,
    ),
    
    height_44 = htres / 100,
    weight_44 = wtres,
  ) %>%
  select(ncdsid, matches("^(h|w)eight_\\d\\d$")) %>%
  pivot_longer(-ncdsid,
               names_pattern = "(.eight)_(..)",
               names_to = c(".value", "fup"),
               names_transform = list(fup = as.integer)) %>%
  mutate(height_20 = ifelse(fup >= 20, height, NA)) %>%
  group_by(ncdsid) %>%
  fill(height_20, .direction = "downup") %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(height = ifelse(fup >= 20 & is.na(height), height_20, height),
         bmi = weight / (height ^ 2),
         obese = ifelse(bmi >= 30, "Obese", "Not Obese") %>%
           factor(c("Not Obese", "Obese"))) %>%
  select(-height_20)

## d. Combine Cleaned Data ----
df_ncds <- reduce(ncds_clean, ~ left_join(.x, .y, by = "ncdsid")) %>%
  relocate(fup, .after = ncdsid) %>%
  rename(iid = ncdsid) %>%
  zap_labels() %>%
  zap_formats() %>%
  set_variable_labels(
    iid = "Individual ID",
    fup = "Follow-Up Age",
    sex = "Sex",
    ethnic_group = "Ethnic Group",
    father_edu_years = "Father's Educational Years",
    mother_edu_years = "Mother's Educational Years",
    father_bmi = "Father's BMI",
    mother_bmi = "Mother's BMI",
    verbal_11 = "Verbal Score @ Age 11y",
    vocab_16 = "Vocabulary Score @ Age 16y",
    height = "Height (m)",
    weight = "Weight (kg)",
    bmi = "Body Mass Index (kg/m^2^)",
    obese = "Obese (BMI ≥ 30 kg/m^2^)"
  )

6.2 MCS

mcs_raw <- list()
mcs_clean <- list()

mcs_fups <- c(0, 3, 5, 7, 11, 14, 17)

load_mcs <- function(file, vars = c()){
  glue("{mcs_fld}/{file}") %>%
    read_dta(col_select = c(matches("^(MCSID|.(C|P)NUM00)$"),
                            all_of(vars)))
}

## a. Sample ----
mcs_raw$xwave <- load_mcs("xwave/mcs_longitudinal_family_file.dta",
                          c("NOCMHH", "DATA_AVAILABILITY"))

mcs_clean$xwave <- mcs_raw$xwave %>%
  filter(DATA_AVAILABILITY == 0) %>%
  uncount(NOCMHH, .id = "CNUM00") %>%
  select(MCSID, CNUM00)

## b. Household Grid ----
# To determine parents and cohort member sex
load_mcs_hhgrid <- function(sweep){
  fup <- mcs_fups[sweep]
  
  glue("{mcs_fld}/{fup}y/mcs{sweep}_hhgrid.dta") %>%
    read_dta(col_select = matches("MCSID|CNUM|CSEX|PNUM|PSEX|CREL")) %>%
    rename(CNUM00 = matches("^.CNUM00"),
           PNUM00 = matches("^.PNUM00"),
           rel = matches("CREL"),
           cm_sex = matches("CSEX"),
           p_sex = matches("PSEX")) %>%
    mutate(sweep = !!sweep,
           .before = 1)
}

  filter(CNUM00 %in% 1:2) %>%
  mutate(sex = negative_to_na(cm_sex) %>%

mcs_clean$parent_grid <- mcs_raw$hhgrid %>%
  filter(rel %in% 7:10) %>% # Natural, adoptive, foster or step-parent.
  mutate(parent_type = case_when(p_sex == 1 ~ "father",

  slice_min(sweep) %>% # First parent of parent type
  slice_min(rel) %>%
  slice(1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%

load_parent_data <- function(sweep){

    read_dta(col_select = matches("MCSID|PNUM|DDBMI00|ACAQ00")) %>%
    rename(PNUM00 = matches("^.PNUM00"),
           bmi_raw = matches("^.DDBMI00"),
           nvq_raw = matches("ACAQ00")) %>%
    mutate(sweep = !!sweep)
}

## f. Cohort Member Cognitive Ability ----
mcs_raw$verbal_11 <- load_mcs("11y/mcs5_cm_derived.dta", "EVSABIL")

mcs_raw$vocab_14 <- load_mcs("14y/mcs6_cm_cognitive_assessment.dta",
                             glue("FCCMCOG{LETTERS[1:20]}"))

clean_vocab_item <- function(item){
  value_labels <- val_labels(item)
  correct_answer <- value_labels[str_detect(names(value_labels), "\\(correct answer\\)")]
  
  case_when(item == correct_answer ~ 1,
            item %in% 1:5 ~ 0)
}

mcs_clean$cog <- mcs_raw$verbal_11 %>%
  full_join(mcs_raw$vocab_14, by = c("MCSID", ECNUM00 = "FCNUM00")) %>%
  mutate(
    verbal_11 = negative_to_na(EVSABIL),
    
    across(matches("FCCMCOG[A-T]"), clean_vocab_item),
    vocab_14 = pick(matches("FCCMCOG[A-T]")) %>% rowSums(na.rm = TRUE),
    vocab_14_obs = pick(matches("FCCMCOG[A-T]")) %>% rowSums(!is.na(.)),
    vocab_14 = ifelse(vocab_14_obs >= 1, vocab_14, NA)
  ) %>%
  select(MCSID, CNUM00 = ECNUM00, verbal_11, vocab_14)

## g. Cohort Member BMI ----
mcs_raw$anthro_3y <- load_mcs("3y/mcs2_cm_interview.dta",
                              c("BCWTKC00", "BCWTGC00", "BCHCMC00", "BCHMMC00"))

load_cm_bmi <- function(sweep){
  fup <- mcs_fups[sweep]
  
  glue("{mcs_fld}/{fup}y/mcs{sweep}_cm_interview.dta") %>%
    read_dta(col_select = matches("MCSID|CNUM|(W|H)TCM(A|0)0")) %>%

           height_raw = matches("^.CHTCM(A|0)0"),
           weight_raw = matches("^.CWTCM(A|0)0")) %>%
    mutate(sweep = !!sweep) 
}

df_mcs <- mcs_clean$xwave %>%
  uncount(length(mcs_fups), .id = "sweep") %>% # To ensure 1 row per sweep for every cohort member
  left_join(mcs_clean$cm_sex, by = c("MCSID", "CNUM00")) %>%
  left_join(mcs_clean$cm_ethnicity, by = c("MCSID", "CNUM00")) %>%

2.1 Vectorisation and Recycling
In this chapter, we provide background on some aspects of R that are pertinent to longitudinal data analyses (LDA). A more detailed introduction to R is provided in the Appendix (to be added forthwith).
R is a vectorised language. This means that operations are applied to entire vectors of data at once, rather than one element at a time in sequence. This makes coding in R very efficient. Below, we add two vectors together, element-wise:
c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5) + c(2, 4, 6, 1, 2)

[1] 3 6 9 5 7
Many functions in R use recycling. This means that if vectors of different lengths are used in an operation, the shorter vector is repeated until it matches the length of the longer vector, even if the longer vector is not a multiple of the shorter one.
c(1, 2, 3) + c(1, 3)

Warning in c(1, 2, 3) + c(1, 3): longer object length is not a multiple of
shorter object length


[1] 2 5 4
Here, c(1, 3) is recycled to c(1, 3, 1) to match the length of c(1, 2, 3). Because this behaviour can be quite surprising, several tidyverse functions do not permit recycling, apart from where the shorter vector has length 1.
In R, one can hold many objects (bits of data) in memory at once. The main data structures you will use in R are vectors, lists, data.frames and tibbles, the tidyverse variant of data.frames.

title: 2  Background on R
text:
2.2 Data Structures
Vectors are sets of values of the same ‘atomic’ type (e.g., integer, double, character, logical).

double: Numbers with ability to store decimal places (e.g. c(2.49, 1, 3/2))
integer: A round number. Denoted using the L operator (e.g. c(1L, 54L, 800L)) .
character: Strings, such as “Hello” and “My name is Liam”.

Strings are surrounded by single (') or double (") quotation marks and can contain quote marks too (e.g. c("Bye", 'Hi', 'He said "Hello"'))

logical: Boolean values TRUE or FALSE
complex: Have limited use, and we will not come across them in this course.

If you try to combine different types of data into a vector, R will coerce them to the same type.

c(1, "two", TRUE)

[1] "1"    "two"  "TRUE"


The atomic type of a vector can be determined using the typeof() function or confirmed using the is.type() set of functions.

typeof(1:3)

[1] "integer"

is.integer(1:3)

[1] TRUE

is.double(1:3)

[1] FALSE

is.numeric(1:3) # Both integer and double are 'numeric'

[1] TRUE


Lists are collections of objects that can collectively be of different types and have different lengths. Lists can also contain other lists and so can be used to represent nested data structures.

list(
  c(1, 2, 3),
  c("a", "b"),
  c(1, "two", TRUE), # Observe: coerced to a character vector
  list(1, "two", TRUE, c(4, 5, 6))
)

[[1]]
[1] 1 2 3

[[2]]
[1] "a" "b"

[[3]]
[1] "1"    "two"  "TRUE"

[[4]]
[[4]][[1]]
[1] 1

[[4]][[2]]
[1] "two"

[[4]][[3]]
[1] TRUE

[[4]][[4]]
[1] 4 5 6


data.frames are two dimensional rectangular structures (like spreadsheets) with columns and rows. data.frames are in fact a special type of list where the columns are sub-objects and the rows are the values at the same position across each of the sub-objects. To be a data.frame, all columns must have the same length - otherwise the data.frame wouldn’t be rectangular. Because they are just special lists, data.frames columns can be other lists (termed list-columns), allowing for nested data structures.

head(iris) # An example data.frame

  Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width Species
1          5.1         3.5          1.4         0.2  setosa
2          4.9         3.0          1.4         0.2  setosa
3          4.7         3.2          1.3         0.2  setosa
4          4.6         3.1          1.5         0.2  setosa
5          5.0         3.6          1.4         0.2  setosa
6          5.4         3.9          1.7         0.4  setosa

title: 2  Background on R
text:
2.3 Subsetting
Subsetting is the process of pulling elements from objects. In R, there are several ways to subset data structures, depending on the object type and the desired outcome.
Vectors can be subsetted using square brackets (‘[ ]’) after the object name, with vectors of integers, logical values or names specified to extract elements. This process creates a new vector. Names and integers can be repeated so the ‘subsetted’ vector is longer than the original one.

ages <- c("Gary" = 10, "Bertie" = 20, "Peter" = 30)
ages[c(3, 2, 1, 1)]

 Peter Bertie   Gary   Gary 
    30     20     10     10 

ages[c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)]

 Gary Peter 
   10    30 

ages[c("Bertie", "Gary")]

Bertie   Gary 
    20     10 


The single square brackets can also be used to subset lists. As with vectors, this in fact creates a new list with the specified elements.

my_list <- list(
  numbers = c(1, 2, 3),
  letters = c("a", "b", "c"),
  mixed = list(1, "two", TRUE)
)
my_list[c(3, 1)]

$mixed
$mixed[[1]]
[1] 1

$mixed[[2]]
[1] "two"

$mixed[[3]]
[1] TRUE


$numbers
[1] 1 2 3


Lists can also be subsetted using double square brackets ([[ ]]) to extract single elements. This returns the actual object stored at that position, rather than a list containing that object. The same behaviour can be obtained using the $ operator with the name of the element one wishes to extract. The $ operator also allows partial name matching.

my_list[2] # Returns a list of length 1.

$letters
[1] "a" "b" "c"

my_list[[2]] # Returns a vector

[1] "a" "b" "c"

my_list$letters

[1] "a" "b" "c"

my_list$lett # Partial matching.

[1] "a" "b" "c"


In the book Advanced R, Hadley Wickham (2023) likens a list to a train engine pulling carriages. [ ] takes the carriages and attaches them to a new engine, while [[ ]] detaches a carriage from the train.
Like lists, data.frames can be subsetted in several ways. The double-square brackets and $ operators extract single columns, while single-square brackets (object[vector]) return a data.frame containing the specified column(s).

my_df <- data.frame(
  name = c("Gary", "Bertie", "Peter"),
  age = c(10, 20, 30),
  score = c(90, 85, 101),
  nationality = factor(c("English", "Scottish", "English"))
)
my_df[[2]] # Extracts the 'age' column as a vector

[1] 10 20 30

my_df["age"] # New data.frame only containing 'age' column

  age
1  10
2  20
3  30


A further option is to use the data.frame[rows, columns] syntax to extract specific rows and columns.

my_df[3:2, c("name", "score")] # Extracts first two rows of 'name' and 'score' columns

    name score
3  Peter   101
2 Bertie    85

my_df[, c("name", "score")] # Extracts all rows of 'name' and 'score' columns

    name score
1   Gary    90
2 Bertie    85
3  Peter   101


Note, data.frames have a peculiar feature where if only one column is specified in the [, ] notation then values are returned as a vector, rather than a (single column) data.frame. As this can lead to unanticipated behaviour, the tibble, which builds upon the data.frame, does not do this:

library(tibble)
my_tibble <- as_tibble(my_df)
my_df[, "age"] # Returns a vector

[1] 10 20 30

my_tibble[, "age"] # Returns a tibble

# A tibble: 3 × 1
    age
  <dbl>
1    10
2    20
3    30


Other differences between tibbles and data.frames will be discussed in the next chapter.
Subsetting operations can be strung together, with the output of one subsetting operation being subsetted further. R reads subsetting operations from left to right.

my_list[["mixed"]][[2]]

[1] "two"


Why am I telling you all this? Well, subsetting is important in general for cleaning data and working with results. One concrete use case is to subset dictionaries to use presentable names for variables and other objects, rather than as stored in a dataset itself. For instance,

variable_dict <- c(age = "Age of Participant", score = "Test Score")
paste("The Average", variable_dict["score"], "is", mean(my_df$score))

[1] "The Average Test Score is 92"

section: 2.4 Constructing Logical and Integer Vectors and the Missing Value
text:
2.4 Constructing Logical and Integer Vectors and the Missing Value
Above we subsetted the ages vector using a logical vector (ages[c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)]). Usually one would not construct logical vectors by hand. Instead, these can be constructed by applying logical operations to vectors.

==: Equal to
!=: Not equal to
<: Less than
>: Greater than
<=: Less than or equal to
>=: Greater than or equal to
%in%: Element of (e.g., ages %in% c(10, 30)).

Note this function is only vectorised on the left hand side.

between(x, lower, upper): x >= lower and x <= upper

For instance:

ages[ages == 25]

named numeric(0)

ages[ages >= 20]

Bertie  Peter 
    20     30 

ages[ages %in% c(10, 30)]

 Gary Peter 
   10    30 


Logical vectors can be combined using the & (AND) or | (OR) operators. The rules for these are: TRUE & TRUE == TRUE, TRUE & FALSE == FALSE, TRUE | FALSE == TRUE, and FALSE | FALSE == FALSE. These operators are vectorised, so they operate element-wise. They are read left to right, unless parentheses are used which take precedence:

ages[ages >= 28 | (ages <= 23 & ages != 20)]

 Gary Peter 
   10    30 


The ! (NOT) operator can be used to negate a logical vector. For instance, !(ages >= 20) is equivalent to ages < 20.
R’s missing value NA is treated literally as “unknown”, so logical operations involving NA return NA. (Think: is an unknown value greater than 5? Well, that is unknown!) An exception to this is the %in% operator which treats NA’s literally and always returns vectors of TRUE or FALSE (i.e., NA %in% c(1, NA) == TRUE). Missing values from a vector can be dropped using na.omit(). The is.na() function can be used to identify NA values.

ages_na <- c(ages, Dave = NA)
ages_na > 20

  Gary Bertie  Peter   Dave 
 FALSE  FALSE   TRUE     NA 

ages_na[ages_na > 20]

Peter  <NA> 
   30    NA 

ages_na[na.omit(ages_na > 20)] # Omits NAs

Peter 
   30 

ages_na[ages_na %in% c(10, NA)]

Gary Dave 
  10   NA 

ages_na[is.na(ages_na)]

Dave 
  NA 


Three functions that can help create integer vectors are which(), match(), seq().

which(logical_vector): Returns the indices where the logical vector equals TRUE.
match(vector, table): Returns a vector of the positions of (first) matches of a vector in another. The function returns NA for non-matches.
seq(from, to, by): Generates a sequence of numbers from from to to, incrementing by by.


which(ages >= 20)

Bertie  Peter 
     2      3 

match(ages, c(30, 10, 40))

[1]  2 NA  1

seq(0, 10, by = 2)

[1]  0  2  4  6  8 10



2.4.1 Task I

Subset the my_list object above to create a new list that contains only the third and first elements (in that order) of the letters sub-object.



Reveal the solution
my_list$letters[c(3, 1)]



Get the name and age of the person with the highest score in my_df.



Reveal the solution
my_df[my_df$score == max(my_df$score), c("name", "age")]

title: 2  Background on R
text:
2.5 Attributes and Generic Functions
Objects in R can be given attributes - metadata providing additional information about the object. We have used one such attribute already above: name. We used this when specifying key-value pairs when creating the vector, list and data.frame objects (e.g., the column names name, age and score in my_df).
Another common attribute is class. As discussed, data structures in R have a specific type (list, character, logical, etc.), but more complex structures can be built on these by specifying their class. For instance, data.frames have the list type (call typeof(my_df)) but the data.frame class. factor vectors (used to store categorical data) are in fact of the integer type (call typeof(my_df$nationality)) but have the factor class along with another another attribute, levels, that determines the labels (and their order) attached to the integers.
An object’s attributes can be viewed using the attributes() function. Specific attributes can be extracted using the attr() function (e.g., attr(my_df, "class")). For common attributes, helper functions to access these attributes exist - e.g., names(), class(), levels(), and dim() (dimensions).1 One important feature of these functions is that they can be used to set attributes as well as get (names(x) <- ...) them.

attr(my_df, "names") # Get column names

[1] "name"        "age"         "score"       "nationality"

names(my_df) <- c("Participant_Name", "Participant_Age", "Test_Score", "Nationality") # Set column names
my_df

  Participant_Name Participant_Age Test_Score Nationality
1             Gary              10         90     English
2           Bertie              20         85    Scottish
3            Peter              30        101     English


An important concept in R is that of generic functions. Generic functions are functions that behave differently depending on the class of the object they are applied to. For instance, the summary() function produces different outputs when applied to a data.frame or to an lm object (the result of fitting a linear model).

summary(my_df)

 Participant_Name   Participant_Age   Test_Score      Nationality
 Length:3           Min.   :10      Min.   : 85.0   English :2   
 Class :character   1st Qu.:15      1st Qu.: 87.5   Scottish:1   
 Mode  :character   Median :20      Median : 90.0                
                    Mean   :20      Mean   : 92.0                
                    3rd Qu.:25      3rd Qu.: 95.5                
                    Max.   :30      Max.   :101.0                

summary(lm(Test_Score ~ Participant_Age, data = my_df))


Call:
lm(formula = Test_Score ~ Participant_Age, data = my_df)

Residuals:
   1    2    3 
 3.5 -7.0  3.5 

Coefficients:
                Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)      81.0000    13.0958   6.185    0.102
Participant_Age   0.5500     0.6062   0.907    0.531

Residual standard error: 8.573 on 1 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.4515,    Adjusted R-squared:  -0.09701 
F-statistic: 0.8231 on 1 and 1 DF,  p-value: 0.5309


This code works because summary() dispatches to different methods depending on the class of the object inputted. One can see the code underlying a function by typing its name without parentheses into the console.

summary

function (object, ...) 
UseMethod("summary")
<bytecode: 0x1344bcd50>
<environment: namespace:base>


Method functions have names of the form: function_name.class_name(). For instance, the summary method for data.frames is summary.data.frame(), while that for linear models it is summary.lm().

summary.data.frame(my_df)

 Participant_Name   Participant_Age   Test_Score      Nationality
 Length:3           Min.   :10      Min.   : 85.0   English :2   
 Class :character   1st Qu.:15      1st Qu.: 87.5   Scottish:1   
 Mode  :character   Median :20      Median : 90.0                
                    Mean   :20      Mean   : 92.0                
                    3rd Qu.:25      3rd Qu.: 95.5                
                    Max.   :30      Max.   :101.0                


Sometimes an object may have multiple classes. In this case, R will search for methods in the order that classes are specified. For instance, tibbles have tbl_df, tbl and data.frame classes. When summary() is applied to a tibble, it first looks for a summary.tbl_df() method. If such a function isn’t found, then R will look for summary.tbl() and, failing that, summary.data.frame(), instead.

class(my_tibble)

[1] "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"


Often method functions are hidden and not directly loaded into the global environment namespace (the set of names associated with objects) - more on namespaces and environments in the next section.

title: 2  Background on R
text:
2.6 Packages, Functions and Environments
As R come bundled with only a limited set of functionality, more can be added using packages. Packages are collections of functions and (less frequently) data that typically revolve around a set of tasks - for instance, the twilio R package can be used to send SMS messages using the Twilio API (helpful if you have a long analysis to run and want to be informed when it is finished). Packages need installing just once (using install.packages("package_name")), but they also loading explicitly into R (library(package_name)) to run in a specific session.
Because R is open-source, anyone can develop or contribute a package. As packages are developed independently, they sometimes do not work together well. For instance, the output of one package’s functions may need reformatting before it can be used in another package’s functions. This decentralised development can also mean that two packages use the same name for entirely different functions. For instance, both the dplyr (part of the tidyverse) and MASS packages have a function called select(). The order in which packages are loaded determines which function is available for immediate use. The most recently loaded package takes precedence - in R parlance, it masks the other one.
Masking means care must be taken when loading packages. One can nevertheless ensure that a specific package’s function is used by prefixing the function name with the package name and two colons (::) or by explicitly saving the specific function into the environment.

library(dplyr)


Attaching package: 'dplyr'


The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':

    filter, lag


The following objects are masked from 'package:base':

    intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

library(MASS) # Masks dplyr::select()


Attaching package: 'MASS'


The following object is masked from 'package:dplyr':

    select

select(my_df, "Test_Score")

Error in `select()`:
! unused argument ("Test_Score")

select <- dplyr::select # Ensures dplyr::select() is used in next line
select(my_df, "Test_Score")

  Test_Score
1         90
2         85
3        101


Note, the double colon (::) operator can also be used to access functions without the package being loaded into the environment. Packages often also contain “non-exported” functions - functions that are only used internally within the package and so are not loaded into the namespace when the package is loaded. The triple colon (:::) operator can be used to access these “non-exported” functions. As mentioned above, this includes many “method” functions.
Given the issue of name conflicts, how does R ensure packages developed independently can be used together at all? This question also arises when considering that objects used internally within functions may have already-used names - for instance, the mean() function uses an object called x, but this is a common name that could easily conflict with user-defined objects.
The answer to the question is that functions have their own environments. Environments are collections of objects (variables and functions) with associated names that R can access. Environments are hierarchical, meaning that if R cannot find an object in the current environment, it will look in the environment’s parent environment, and, if that fails, the parent environment of that, and so on. The parent environment of a function is the environment in which the function was defined.
The environment when working at the R console is known as the global environment. The global environment, which is the environment where user-defined objects and functions are stored, is the parent environment of the functions created in that environment. Below the global environment are the environments of loaded packages (in reverse order of their loading), followed by the “Base” environment, which contains the core R functions, and which are loaded automatically when R opens.
What this means is that when a function is called, R searches for it - and any objects used in the function - in the calling environment first and then down the heirarchy. So, if another MASS function calls select(), it will reliably call MASS::select(), even if dplyr is loaded later. Further, if the package uses (or creates) an object called (e.g.) x, it will be the object x within the function environment (or lower down the hierarchy), rather than any object x in the global environment.
Below, we create a strange function, add_1(), that adds 1 to an object y, which isn’t defined in the function but is defined in the global environment, which is the parent of the function environment. and stores this in an the object x, which shares the name of an object already defined in the global environment. Notice that (a) add_1() returns 16 as y = 15 in the global environment, (b) the object x in the global environment remains unchanged (x = 3), and (c) add_1() does not error, despite z not being inputted when the function is called - this last observation is because R uses lazy evaluation and z is not called in the function body.

x <- 3
y <- 15
add_1 <- function(z){
  x <- y + 1
  return(x)
}
add_1()

[1] 16

x

[1] 3


add_1() shows the three elements of functions in R. Specifically, functions have a name (add_1), a set of arguments (inputs; z), and a body containing the code that is performed by the function (x <- y + 1; return(x)). Note, default values can be given to arguments in the function definition (e.g., z = 1). Some function pass on arguments to other functions or take an indeterminate number of arguments - for instance, the c() function can create vectors from any number of inputs. Functions like this typically use ... syntax for some arguments.

2.8 .Rproj and Environment Variables
An .Rproj file is a project file used by RStudio to manage and organize R projects. Double-clicking on an .Rproj file will open RStudio and set the working directory to the location of the project. This is useful for keeping all files related to a specific project in one place. It also means that relative, rather than absolute, file paths can be used when reading and writing files, which is better for security and reproducibility.
You may wish to keep some files separate to the project folder - for instance, it can make sense to have one central copy of raw data, if it will be used in multiple projects. As these files will be stored separately, you won’t be able to use relative file paths to open them and - again for data security reasons - you may not wish to specify full file paths in the code you create (or share). A solution to this is to use environment variables. Environment variables are key-value pairs that are loaded into R on start-up from .Renviron files.
R automatically looks for a .Renviron file in the working directory (i.e., the project folder) and in the user’s home directory. You can create a .Renviron file in your project folder to specify environment variables specific to that project. In this course, we will use environment variables to store file paths to the NCDS and MCS datasets. This way, we can keep the actual file paths for these datasets hidden.
You can create and edit a project .Renviron file within your working directory by calling usethis::edit_r_environ("project") .Renviron files are plain text files where each line contains a key-value pair in the format KEY=VALUE. Environment variables can then be called within the R session by calling Sys.getenv("KEY").

mcs_fld <- Sys.getenv("mcs_fld")
ncds_fld <- Sys.getenv("ncds_fld")

Please call usethis::edit_r_environ("project") now and edit the .Renviron file to include lines for mcs_fld and ncds_fld. These should point at the top directories from which the sweep-specific data folders are stored - i.e., the folder that looks as below:

title: 3  An Introduction to the tidyverse
text:
3.1 The tidyverse Philosophy
The tidyverse is a collection of packages that cover most of the central tasks of data science, from opening data files, to cleaning variables, producing descriptive and inferential statistics, and presenting results in tables and plots. The tidyverse is developed by Hadley Wickham and colleagues at Posit (the developers of RStudio). The main tidyverse packages can be installed using the install.packages("tidyverse") function. Calling library(tidyverse) loads the “core” tidyverse packages, a subset of those installed by install.packages("tidyverse"). The “core” tidyverse packages are ggplot2, dplyr, tidyr, readr, purrr, tibble, stringr, forcats, and lubridate. Collectively, these cover the most common data science tasks, but we will need to load a few extra, as and when. Note, some of the core packages also load specific functions from other tidyverse packages (notably the magrittr %>% pipe operator; see next section).
# install.packages("tidyverse")
library(tidyverse)
tidyverse packages work seamlessly together because they follow a common design philosophy. As this philosophy is public and well-documented, other developers can write packages that fit within the tidyverse ecosystem (and do). The two main features of the tidyverse philosophy are incrementalism and tidy data.

title: 3  An Introduction to the tidyverse
text:
3.1.1 Incrementalism (and the %>% pipe)
tidyverse functions are generally designed to do one thing. If a function requires data to be prepared in a specific way, it is typically expected this will be done prior using separate functions. tidyverse functions have simple descriptive ‘verb’ as names - for instance, select() to choose columns from a tibble, filter() to retain specific rows, and mutate() to add or edit columns. This single-purpose philosophy makes it easier to read and write tidyverse code as decomposes complex processes into a sequence of relatively simple steps.
To facilitate incrementalism, the tidyverse makes heavy use of the pipe (%>%) operator (from magrittr). The pipe works as follows: it takes the object produced on its left hand side and puts it into the first argument of the function on its right hand side. This is best explained by example:

c(1, 2, 3) %>% mean()

[1] 2


In this command, R first creates the vector c(1, 2, 3) then puts it into the first argument of the mean() function.
Pipes can be chained together. For instance:

c(1, 2, 3) %>% 
  mean() %>% 
  paste("is the mean value")

[1] "2 is the mean value"


A series of pipe operations can be read as “do this, then do this, then do this…”. Observe that the above is easier to read than:

paste(mean(c(1,2,3)), "is the mean value")

To be compatible with the pipe operator, tidyverse functions are designed to take the data to be operated on as their first argument. Note, sometimes (particularly when using non-tidyverse functions), the relevant argument is not the first. In which case, one can use the dot (.) placeholder within the function call to indicate where the piped object should go.1 For instance:

c(1, 2, 3) %>% 
  mean() %>%
  paste("The mean value is", .)

[1] "The mean value is 2"




3.1.2 Tidy Data
The second main feature of the tidyverse philosophy is tidy data. As noted, most tidyverse functions are designed to take data as their first input and many output data, too. tidyverse functions generally operate on tibbles, with the expectation they are structured in a tidy way. Tidy data is data where each variable is in its own column, each observation is in its own row, and each value is in its own cell - in LDA settings, this generally means “long format”, with one row per person-sweep, though we will see other structures in the course, too. Tidy data is useful because it work works well with R’s vectorised structure. More on tidy data can be read in Wickham (2014).


3.1.3 A Warning: Continuous Development
The tidyverse is under continuous development, and the developers are predisposed to tinker, withdrawing or retiring functions that no longer fit with their (developing) philosophy. They are also opinionated, choosing to restrict functions to encourage safe practices (for instance, in the last chapter, we saw how tibbles do not use recycling of vectors of length greater than 1). It is advisable to keep up to date with changes to the tidyverse. The tidyverse blog is a good place to start.


3.1.4 Task I

How could the following command be written using the (%>%) pipe?


paste("The sum of unique values in c(1, 3, 3, 1) is", 
      sum(unique(c(1, 3, 3, 1))))



Reveal the solution
c(1, 3, 3, 1) %>%
  unique() %>%
  sum() %>%
  paste("The sum of unique values in c(1, 3, 3, 1) is", .)

title: 3  An Introduction to the tidyverse
text:
3.2 Some Useful tidyverse Functions
There are several tidyverse functions we will use repeatedly in this course. We’ll introduce these here, and discuss more advanced ways of using them in later sessions.

3.2.1 glue::glue()
Above we constructed a string from R objects using paste(). The glue package (a non-core tidyverse package) provides multiple functions for constructing strings, but with more user-friendly interfaces. 3.2.3 tibble::tibble()
As discussed, tibbles are the tidyverse’s version of data.frames. They differ from data.frames in a few key ways:

They do not convert character vectors to factors by default.
They do not allow partial matching of column names when using the $ operator.
They have a cleaner print() method that shows only the first 10 rows and as many columns as fit on the screen.
They do not use recycling of vectors of length greater than 1 when assigning values to columns.
Subsetting a tibble with [rows, columns] syntax always returns a tibble

tibbles can be created from scratch using the tibble function and data.frames can be converted to tibbles using the as_tibble() function. A nice characteristic of the tibble function is that columns just created can be used to create other columns within the same function call.

tibble(
  x = 1:3,
  y = x^2,
  z = y + 2
)

1     1     1     3
2     2     4     6
3     3     9    11


The tibble package contains a few other helpful functions, including:

tribble(): for creating small tibbles in a row-wise fashion.
enframe() and deframe(): for converting named vectors or lists to tibbles and vice-versa.
as_tibble_row(): for converting vectors to single-row tibbles.

3.2.6 dplyr::mutate()
The mutate() function is used to create new - or overwrite existing - columns in a tibble. The new column can be a function of other columns, and can be used to make other columns within the same function call. Below we create two new columns for age-squared and BMI multiplied by age-squared. Unlike filter(), mutate() works sequentially.

mcs_17y_mini %>%
  mutate(age_sq = GCMCS7AG^2,
         bmi_x_age_sq = GCBMIN7*age_sq)

A helpful function to use within the mutate() function is ifelse(). The value ifelse() returns depends on whether a Boolean expression is TRUE or FALSE for a given observation. Below we create two new variables, bmi and obese. The former contains the values of GCBMIN7 with negative values recorded as missing. The latter is a binary variable equal to 1 if the individual’s BMI is greater than 30, and 0 otherwise.

mcs_17y_mini %>%
  mutate(bmi = ifelse(bmi >= 0, GCBMIN7, NA),
         obese = ifelse(bmi >= 30, 1, 0)) %>%
  select(GCBMIN7, bmi, obese)

Note, NAs are propagated through ifelse() (i.e., if bmi is NA, then obese will also be NA).
More complex decision rules can be implemented with the dplyr::case_when() function. This sets the value for an element depending on which of a series of conditions is met. We can use this can to create a BMI category variable and handle the negative value missing codes correctly.

mcs_17y_mini %>%
  mutate(
    bmi_category = case_when(
      GCBMIN7 < 0 ~ NA,
      GCBMIN7 < 18.5 ~ "Underweight",
      GCBMIN7 >= 18.5 & GCBMIN7 < 25 ~ "Normal weight",
      GCBMIN7 >= 25 & GCBMIN7 < 30 ~ "Overweight",
      GCBMIN7 >= 30 ~ "Obese",
      TRUE ~ NA
    )
  ) %>%
  select(GCBMIN7, bmi_category)

  mutate(bmi = ifelse(bmi >= 0, bmi, NA)) %>%
  drop_na(bmi) %>%
  group_by(region) %>%
  summarise(mean_bmi = mean(bmi),
            sd_bmi = sd(bmi)) %>%
  ungroup()



One definition of an outlier is a value more than 3 SD outside the mean. Count the number of outliers in each region. How many outliers does the region with the second highest proportion of observations that are outliers have?



Reveal the solution
ncds_55y_mini %>%
  mutate(bmi = ifelse(bmi >= 0, bmi, NA)) %>%
  drop_na(bmi) %>%
  group_by(region) %>%
  mutate(
    mean_bmi = mean(bmi),
    sd_bmi = sd(bmi),
    outlier = ifelse(bmi < (mean_bmi - 3*sd_bmi) |
                       bmi > (mean_bmi + 3*sd_bmi), 1, 0)
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    n_total = n(),
    n_outliers = sum(outlier),
    prop_outliers = n_outliers / n_total
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(prop_outliers)) %>%
  slice(3)





3.2.11 purrr::map()
Often, you will need to apply the same operation to a similar set of objects - for instance, you may wish to load multiple datasets, to clean several variables in the same way, or to run many regression models (e.g., varying the outcomes or sets of covariates). Writing this out for each object separately is time-consuming, error-prone and not adaptable to changes.
The purrr package (a core tidyverse package) provides a suite of functions for repeating yourself in R. The main function map() takes two arguments: a set of objects one wishes to repeat a function for, and the function to be repeated. map() function calls can be written in a few different ways, but in this course we will predominantly use ‘lambda’ notation. Below, we use map() to open three MCS datasets and to calculate the number of rows in each.

  "mcs1_family_derived.dta",
  "mcs1_parent_derived.dta") %>%
  map(
    ~ glue("{mcs_fld}/0y/{.x}") %>%
      read_dta() %>%
      nrow()
  )

[[2]]
[1] 18540

[1] 33884


In this map() call, .x stands as a placeholder for current value of the object being looped over. When passed a vector, map() loops over each element of the vector in turn, so in first case, .x = "mcs1_cm_derived.dta", in the second case, .x = "mcs1_family_derived.dta", and in the third case, .x = "mcs1_parent_derived.dta". Each time, map() takes the current value of .x, inserts it into the glue() function, reads in the relevant dataset, and calculates the number of rows.
For tibbles, map() loops over columns. If you unsure how map() splits a particular object, map(.x, ~ .x) will return the inputs back, split whichever way they have been.
map() always returns a list. If the input is named, the output will be named, too. There are variants of map() that return other object types. For instance:

map_dbl() returns a numeric vector
map_int() returns an integer vector
map_chr() returns a character vector
map_lgl() returns a logical vector
map_dfr() returns a tibble appending the results together by row (with dplyr::bind_rows()).
map_dfr() returns a tibble joining the results together by column (with dplyr::bind_cols()).

map() only loops over a single input. map2() (and its variants) loop over two inputs, side by side. Its syntax is similar to map() but uses two placeholders, .x and .y (i.e., map2(.x, .y, ~ f(.x, .y))). pmap() (and its variants) generalise this still further to multiple inputs. Instead of .x or .y as placeholders, it uses ..1, ..2, and so on. pmap() takes a list of inputs as its first argument (pmap(list(..1, ..2, ...), ~ f(..1, ..2, ...)).
purrr also contains other useful functions, including reduce(), which we will see later in this course.

3.2.11.1 Task IV

Using a relevant variant of map_*(), identify the number of MCS cohort members interviewed each sweep by opening the mcsx_cm_interview.dta datasets and counting the number of rows, outputted to an integer vector. To help, we provide a dictionary to find the folder for a given sweep (e.g., the 6th sweep was at age 14y).


mcs_fups <- c(0, 3, 5, 7, 11, 14, 17)



Reveal the solution
map_int(
  1:7,
  ~ glue("{mcs_fld}/{mcs_fups[.x]}y/mcs{.x}_cm_interview.dta") %>%
    read_dta() %>%
    nrow()
)

text:
3.3 Putting It All Together
We have intimated at some of the complexity that can be achieved with the tidyverse by piping individual functions together. Below, we chain several to identify cohort members who have appeared in each sweep of the MCS and find to the difference in mean BMI between sweeps 6 and 7 among this balanced panel, using less than twenty lines of code. We use a tidyselect helper, matches(), to select some columns based on a regular expression - used alongside col_select(), this loads a variable if it matches the regular expression, and doesn’t crash if not matching variables are found. We delay discussing matches() and regular expressions until later chapters.

map_dfr(
  1:7,
  ~ glue("{mcs_fld}/{mcs_fups[.x]}y/mcs{.x}_cm_derived.dta") %>%
    read_dta(col_select = c("MCSID", matches("^([A-G]CNUM00|GCBMIN7|FCBMIN6)$"))) %>%
    rename(CNUM = matches("^[A-G]CNUM00$")),
  .id = "wave"
) %>%
  add_count(MCSID, CNUM) %>%
  filter(n == 7) %>%
  mutate(bmi = case_when(
    FCBMIN6 >= 0 ~ FCBMIN6,
    GCBMIN7 >= 0 ~ GCBMIN7
  )
  ) %>%
  drop_na(bmi) %>%
  group_by(wave) %>%
  summarise(mean_bmi = mean(bmi)) %>%
  mutate(diff_mean_bmi = mean_bmi - lag(mean_bmi))

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  wave  mean_bmi diff_mean_bmi
  <chr>    <dbl>         <dbl>
1 6         21.3         NA   
2 7         23.2          1.86

title: 4  Data Discovery
text:
4.1 Creating Codebooks using codebookr::codebook()
A sine qua non of longitudinal research is working out what variables are available in a given study, what their values indicate, and in which data files the variables are stored. This can be a surprisingly time-consuming process, but can be made more efficient using R. In this chapter, we will look at three packages for exploring data files: codebookr,labelled and summarytools. We will also look at stringr for working with character vectors.
The raw data are in Stata (.dta) format, so we will load them using the read_dta() function from the haven package. Let’s load the tidyverse and haven packages, as well as codebook, labelled, summarytools and glue, the latter of which we’ll use to construct file paths. Let’s also load the cohort member derived variable dataset from Sweep 7 (17y) of the MCS:
We can start by creating a codebook using the codebook() function from codebookr. This is straightforward and involves two steps. First, creating the codebook as an R object. Second, saving the codebook as a Word (.docx) document. The R object isn’t useful in itself. It is the .docx file that we will use.
mcs_17y_codebook <- codebook(mcs_cm_derived_17y)
print(mcs_17y_codebook, "outputs/mcs7_cm_derived_codebook.docx")
Below is a screenshot of the results. You can open the generated Word document to view the full codebook.
The resulting .docx contains information on each variable including metadata such as variable labels, value labels, and basic descriptive statistics (e.g., mean, standard deviation, min, max, number of missing values). UKDS files typically come bundled with data dictionaries, but these can be limited (for instance, not including descriptive statistics), and so codebookr outputs can be better to work with.
There is some customisation possible within the codebook() function - see the help file (?codebook) for more information. Note, codebook() can take a while to run, especially for larger datasets.

title: 4  Data Discovery
text:
4.2 Searching Datasets with labelled::lookfor()
An issue with the codebook() output is that, being outside R, one cannot search through it programmatically using R functions. The lookfor() function from the labelled package provides such functionality. labelled is not part of the tidyverse, but does follow its design philosophy.
lookfor() has a simple interface - you provide a data.frame (or tibble) and a search string or set of search strings. The function then identifies variables that match any of these strings, searching not just in the variable names, but also in variable and value labels. For instance, to find variables related to “overweight” in mcs_cm_derived_17y, we can enter the following:

lookfor(mcs_cm_derived_17y, "overweight")

 pos variable label                   col_type missing values                 
 4   GCOVWGT7 Overweight Cut-Off poi~ dbl+lbl  0       [-1] Not applicable    
 7   GCOVWTU7 Overweight cut-Off poi~ dbl+lbl  0       [-1] Not applicable    
 10  GCOBFLG7 MCS7 Obesity flag - IO~ dbl+lbl  0       [-1] Not applicable    
                                                       [0] Not overweight (in~
                                                       [1] Overweight         
                                                       [2] Obese              
 11  GCUK90O7 MCS7 Obesity flag - UK~ dbl+lbl  0       [-1] Not applicable    
                                                       [1] Underweight        
                                                       [2] Healthy weight     
                                                       [3] Overweight         
                                                       [4] Obese              


This function call returned information on four variables. By default, the search is not case-sensitive, behaviour that can be changed by setting the argument ignore.case = FALSE. The labels and values arguments can also be changed to exclude these metadata from the search. Note, calling lookfor() without specifying a search string will return information on all variables in the dataset.
Converting lookfor() output into a tibble (with as_tibble()) allows one to use dplyr functions to search the output further still. Here, we use the str_detect() function from stringr to keep only those rows that contain “IOTF” in the variable label:

lookfor(mcs_cm_derived_17y, "overweight") %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  filter(str_detect(label, "IOTF"))

# A tibble: 2 × 7
    pos variable label                      col_type missing levels value_labels
  <int> <chr>    <chr>                      <chr>      <int> <name> <named list>
1     4 GCOVWGT7 Overweight Cut-Off point … dbl+lbl        0 <NULL> <dbl [1]>   
2    10 GCOBFLG7 MCS7 Obesity flag - IOTF … dbl+lbl        0 <NULL> <dbl [4]>   


You will notice this output returns two columns that are lists (the list-columns levels and value_label). We will return to list-columns later.
The lookfor() function uses regular expressions for search strings. Regular expressions are a compact way of specifying patterns in text. The syntax can be hard to remember as well as to read. Guides are available online, and ChatGPT can be especially helpful here. Nevertheless, the most useful rules are worth committing to memory because they get used a lot:

The ^ and $ symbols are used to anchor the start and the end of a string respectively. For instance, ^age matches any string that starts with “age”, while age$ matches any string that ends with “age”. ^age$ matches any string that is exactly “age”.
The . symbol matches any single character. For instance, a.e matches “age”, “axe”, “are”, etc.
The * symbol matches zero or more occurrences of the preceding character. For instance, a* matches “a”, “aa”, etc. The combination .* matches any sequence of characters (e.g., a.*e matches “ae”, “ace”, “apple”, etc.).
The | symbol is used for logical OR. For instance, age|weight matches any string that contains either “age” or “weight”. Specified in parentheses, it can be used to group patterns (e.g., (mother|father)_(education|age) matches “mother_education”, “father_age”, “mother_age” and “father_education”).
The \ symbol is used to escape special characters. A quirk of R is that you need to escape special characters twice. For instance, to match a literal dollar ($), you would use \\$ in your regular expression.
The [] symbols are used to specify a set of characters. [0-9] matches any digit, [a-z] matches any lowercase letter, [A-Z] matches any uppercase letter, and [aeiou] matches any lowercase vowel. The [^] syntax can be used to specify a set of characters to exclude. For instance, [^0-9] matches any character that is not a digit.
The \\d, \\s, and \\w symbols are shorthand for digits, whitespace and ‘word characters’ (digits, letters, or underscores), respectively.

Regular expressions are also used within the stringr package. For instance, str_detect(label, "IOTF") above returned a logical vector equal TRUE where the variable label contained “IOTF”.
Note, the labelled package also contains several helper functions for getting or setting attributes from labelled data. This includes:

var_labels() to extract variable labels for a tibble or from a vector.
set_variable_labels() to set variable labels for a tibble.
val_labels() to extract value labels.

Find variables related to obesity or BMI in the mcs_cm_derived_17y dataset. Consider that the variable label may use related but different terms to these exact expressions.



Reveal the solution
lookfor(mcs_cm_derived_17y, "obese|mass|bmi") # Multiple terms to capture variations

text:
4.3 Data Overviews with summarytools::dfSummary()
Another useful function for exploring datasets is dfSummary() from summarytools (not part of the tidyverse). This function provides a report on each variable in a dataset, like codebook() adding information on basic descriptive statistics, number of missing values, variable and value labels and so on. It also helpfully provided a histogram of values for each variable. The output can be viewed in the R console or alternatively in the R viewer pane by calling stview() on the dfSummary() output.

# OUTPUT NOT SHOWN
mcs_17y_summary <- dfSummary(mcs_cm_derived_17y)
stview(mcs_17y_summary)

dfSummary() is useful alongside lookfor() as it can help inform data cleaning. However dfSummary() is limited with labelled data because it does not display value labels for continuous variables (which can include values that are in fact missing codes; e.g., negative numbers). Several alternatives to dfSummary() exist which also have limitations with labelled data, including skimr::skim() and dlookr::diagnose_web_report(). dplyr::count() is very useful with labelled data as labels are presented within tibble printed outputs.

mcs_cm_derived_17y %>%
  count(GCOBFLG7)

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  GCOBFLG7                                        n
  <dbl+lbl>                                   <int>
1 -1 [Not applicable]                          1529
2  0 [Not overweight (including underweight)]  6628
3  1 [Overweight]                              1806
4  2 [Obese]                                    989


Given negative values (with few exceptions - e.g., income) are reserved for missing codes in the raw data, one way around this is to do some basic cleaning to replace negative values with NA. We did this in the last session using the ifelse() and case_when() functions. However, an issue is they do not retain metadata. Instead, we can use functionality from the labelled package. Below we create a function negative_to_na() which uses the labelled::na_range() and labelled::user_na_to_na().

# OUTPUT NOT SHOWN
negative_to_na <- function(x){
  na_range(x) <- c(-Inf, -1)
  user_na_to_na(x)
}

mcs_cm_derived_17y %>%
  mutate(bmi_cat_ifelse = ifelse(GCOBFLG7 >= 0, GCOBFLG7, NA),
         bmi_cat_cleaned = negative_to_na(GCOBFLG7)) %>%
  select(GCOBFLG7, bmi_cat_ifelse, bmi_cat_cleaned) %>%
  dfSummary() %>%
  stview()

In the next chapter, we will see how to apply the negative_to_na() function across multiple variables at once using dplyr::across().

text:
4.5 Loading Data from Data Dictionaries
Given it contains information of file paths, the data dictionaries can be used to load specific variables. Here the key is to create a smaller tibble which has one row per file to be loaded and contains the information needed to construct a file path plus the vector of variables one wishes to import. To do this, we can use the tidyr::chop() function to collapse down multiple rows per file into a single row, with a list-column containing the variables to import.

mcs_dict_clean %>%
  filter(str_detect(label_low, "iotf")) %>% 
  select(fld, file, variable) %>% 
  chop(variable)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  fld   file                   variable
  <chr> <chr>               <list<chr>>
1 14y   mcs6_cm_derived.dta         [3]
2 17y   mcs7_cm_derived.dta         [3]


Note, these variables aren’t helpful on their own because they need to be loaded with identifier variables to make sure the data can be ascribed to an observational unit (e.g., a cohort member). In the next step, we load the data using read_dta(), specifying the col_select argument, including relevant identifier variables.

load_from_dict <- function(fld, file, variables){
  glue("{mcs_fld}/{fld}/{file}") %>%
    read_dta(col_select = c("MCSID", matches("^.CNUM00$"), all_of(variables)))
}

mcs_dict_clean %>%
  filter(str_detect(label_low, "iotf")) %>% 
  select(fld, file, variable) %>% 
  chop(variable) %>%
  mutate(data = pmap(list(fld, file, variable), load_from_dict))

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  fld   file                   variable data                 
  <chr> <chr>               <list<chr>> <list>               
1 14y   mcs6_cm_derived.dta         [3] <tibble [11,859 × 5]>
2 17y   mcs7_cm_derived.dta         [3] <tibble [10,952 × 5]>


If we just wanted the data itself, we could have further called ... %>% select(file, data) %>% deframe() to return a named list of datasets.
In the col_select argument we use two tidyselect helpers:

matches() finds variables which match a regular expression. (XCNUM00 is used in each sweep to identify cohort members, with X a letter indicating sweep.)
all_of() selects all variables in a character vector.

We will return to tidyselect helpers in the next chapter.

4.5.1 Task IV

Adapt the load_from_dict() function to load NCDS variables related to height in the Age 55y sweep. NCDSID is the cohort member identifier in the NCDS. In some datasets, it is in upper case. In others, lower case. Bonus: try to make the function flexible enough that it can work with both MCS and NCDS data dictionaries.



Reveal the solution
load_from_dict_v2 <- function(fld, file, variables, 
                                study_fld = ncds_fld,
                                id_regex = "NCDSID|ncdsid"){
  glue("{study_fld}/{fld}/{file}") %>%
    read_dta(col_select = c(matches(id_regex), all_of(variables)))
}

ncds_data_dict %>%
  filter(fld == "55y",
         str_detect(label_low, "height")) %>% 
  select(fld, file, variable) %>% 
  chop(variable) %>%
  mutate(data = pmap(list(fld, file, variable), load_from_dict_v2))

title: 5  Preparing Data for Analysis
text:
5.1 Advanced Functions for Data Cleaning
In Chapter 3, we saw the main functions of the tidyverse. In this chapter, we will explore advanced uses of these functions, as well as introduce further functions for merging and reshaping tibbles, key steps in LDA. The aim is to make analysis-ready datasets in as efficient a manner as possible.
The packages we will use are:
We’ll begin using data from the MCS Sweep 7 (17y) cohort member interview dataset.

title: 5  Preparing Data for Analysis
text:
5.1.1 tidyselect Helpers
In Chapter 3, we used select() to retain or drop variables from a tibble. We saw the manual way of doing this (specifying each variable separately), as well as a more programmatic way: using a tidyselect helper, matches(), that selected every variable whose name matched a regular expression. matches() is one of many tidyselect helpers:

matches(): selects variables based on regular expressions (e.g., matches("^G") selects any variable starting "G").
x:y: selects variables location between x and y (inclusive). x and y can be variable names and/or positions. last_col() is another useful helper that can be used in this context (e.g., age:last_col() selects every column from age to the last column).
where(): selects variables based on a logical condition - this condition is applied to the values not the variable names. For example, where(is.factor) selects all factor variables.
all_of(): selects all variables specified in a character vector (e.g., all_of(c("sex", "age") selects columns sex and age). Note, all_of() throws an error if not all of the specified variables are present in the tibble.
any_of(): returns any variables specified in a character vector that are available in a tibble. Unlike all_of(), any_of() does not throw an error if a specified variable is not present.
everything(): selects every column in a tibble. This may seem redundant, but we will see contexts in which it is useful.

tidyselect helpers can be combined with the & (AND) and | (OR) operators, while the ! (NOT) operator can be used to identify variables that do not meet a condition. For example, where(is.numeric) & !matches("^G") selects all numeric variables that do not start "G". Below is some example code.

Question: Which variables will remain in the outputted tibble?


mcs_17y %>%
  select(matches("^GCW")) %>%
  select(GCWESM00:last_col()) %>%
  select(where(is.labelled)) %>%
  select(all_of(c("GCWWOP00", "GCWWUS00", "GCWWRE00"))) %>%
  select(any_of(c("GCWWOP00", "GCWWRE00", "not_a_variable"))) %>%
  select(!matches("^GCWWO"))

# A tibble: 10,345 × 1
   GCWWRE00            
   <dbl+lbl>           
 1 2 [Rarely]          
 2 3 [Some of the time]
 3 2 [Rarely]          
 4 4 [Often]           
 5 2 [Rarely]          
 6 1 [None of the time]
 7 4 [Often]           
 8 4 [Often]           
 9 2 [Rarely]          
10 3 [Some of the time]
# ℹ 10,335 more rows


tidyselect helpers can be used in many functions in the tidyverse beyond select(). For instance, they can be used to specify columns in drop_na(), in the col_select = ... argument of read_dta(), in the .cols = ... argument of rename_with(), and in across() (more on which below).
tidyselect helpers are not just useful for selecting raw variables en masse, but can also be used with cleaned variables too. This is made easier if care is taken to name cleaned variables consistently. For instance, naming BMI variables in a ‘wide’ dataset in a consistent way (e.g., bmi_03, bmi_05, …, bmi_17) allows one to use a simple regular expression (matches("^bmi_\\d\\d$")) to select them. Later, we will use vectors that specify control variables to be used in regression models and select them with all_of().


5.1.2 dplyr::rename_with()
Variables can be renamed en masse using rename_with(). rename_with() applies a function to each variable name in turn. Functions can be specified using the lambda notation we used in Chapter 3 with purrr:map(). The stringr package contains several functions that can be used inside rename_with, including str_replace() (to replace part of a string with another string), str_remove() (to remove part of a string), str_to_lower() (to put strings in lower case), and str_sub() (to extract characters between specified positions in a string; e.g., str_sub(x, 2, -2) extracts the second to penultimate letters of x). glue::glue() can also be handy. Here are some examples:

mcs_17y %>%
  rename_with(str_to_lower) %>% # Equivalent to ~ str_to_lower(.x)
  rename_with(~ str_remove(.x, "^g")) %>%  # Removes sweep-specific prefix "G"
  rename_with(~ glue("{.x}_17"),
              .cols = -c(mcsid, cnum00))

Notice the line rename_with(str_to_lower) - when just a function name is specified, the column will be placed in the first argument of that function. This syntax can also be used in purrr::map(). Note, rename_with(~ str_remove(.x, "^G")) is an essential preparatory step if one wishes to append data from different sweeps of the MCS together.


5.1.3 Task I

Open the age 50y and 62y main interview files (ncds_2008_followup.dta and ncds10_age62_main_interview.dta, respectively). Use tidyselect helpers to select every derived variable in these datasets.



Reveal the solution
ncds_50y <- glue("{ncds_fld}/50y/ncds_2008_followup.dta") %>% 
  read_dta() 
ncds_62y <- glue("{ncds_fld}/62y/ncds10_age62_main_interview.dta") %>% 
  read_dta()

lookfor(ncds_50y, "derived")
lookfor(ncds_62y, "derived")

ncds_50y %>%
  select(NCDSID, matches("ND8"))

ncds_62y %>%
  select(ncdsid, matches("nd10"))



Consider how to rename the variables in both datasets so that they could be appended together.



Reveal the solution
names(ncds_50y)
names(ncds_62y)

harmonise_names <- function(df){
  df %>%
    rename_with(str_to_lower) %>%
    rename_with(~ str_remove(.x, "^nd(8|10)") %>%
                  paste0("_derived"),
                .cols = matches("^nd(8|10)")) %>%
    rename_with(~ str_remove(.x, "^n(8|10)"),
                .cols = -matches("_derived$"))
}

harmonise_names(ncds_50y)
harmonise_names(ncds_62y)




5.1.4 dplyr::across()
across() allows one to apply a function to multiple variables in turn. It is most typically used in mutate() to transform multiple variables in the same way. A key use of across() in LDA is to replace negative values representing missing codes with R’s NA missing value. In Chapter 3, we used ifelse() to recode negative values, but this drops variable metadata (e.g., value labels) that we may wish to keep. To recode missing values while retaining other metadata, we can use functionality from the labelled package as in the negative_to_na() function below. We apply this to all labelled variables (where(is.labelled)) using across().

negative_to_na <- function(x){
  na_range(x) <- c(-Inf, -1)
  user_na_to_na(x)
}

mcs_17y %>%
  select(MCSID, GCNUM00, matches("^GCHT(CM|FT|IN)00")) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.labelled), ~ negative_to_na(.x)))

# A tibble: 10,345 × 5

   <chr>   <dbl+lbl>                           <dbl+lbl> <dbl+lbl> <dbl+lbl>
 1 M10002P 1 [1st Cohort Member of the family] 174.      NA        NA       
 2 M10007U 1 [1st Cohort Member of the family] 181.       5        11       
 3 M10015U 1 [1st Cohort Member of the family] 169        5         6       
 4 M10016V 1 [1st Cohort Member of the family] 185.       6         0       
 5 M10018X 1 [1st Cohort Member of the family] 166.       5         5       
 6 M10021S 1 [1st Cohort Member of the family] 157.       5         1       
 7 M10022T 1 [1st Cohort Member of the family] 185.       6         0       
 8 M10025W 1 [1st Cohort Member of the family] 191        6         3       
 9 M10034X 1 [1st Cohort Member of the family] 179.       5        10       
10 M10041W 1 [1st Cohort Member of the family]  NA       NA        NA       
# ℹ 10,335 more rows


By default, mutate(across()) overwrites the original variables. New columns can be created instead by specifying a named list of functions. The .names argument of across() allows one to also specify a rubric for the new columns names and uses glue()-like syntax.

mcs_17y %>%
  select(matches("^GCHT(CM|FT|IN)00")) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.labelled), ~ negative_to_na(.x))) %>%
  summarise(across(where(is.numeric),
                   list(mean = ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
                        sd = ~ sd(.x, na.rm = TRUE)),

5.1.5 Some Helpful Functions for Labelled Data
Sometimes, in longitudinal datasets, certain positive values can indicate missingness, particularly in the context of a specific analysis. For instance, some self-complete items in the Sweep 7 of the MCS use positive values for responses that could be considered missing (e.g., “Don’t know” or “Prefer not to say”). Specific values can be replaced with NA using the code below. This code also uses haven::as_factor(), which converts labelled vectors to factors using the value labels as levels.

values_to_na <- function(x, values){
  na_values(x) <- values
  user_na_to_na(x)
}

  mutate(self_rated_health = negative_to_na(GCCGHE00) %>%

5.1.6 dplyr::if_any() / dplyr::if_all()
if_any() and if_all() are similar to across() in that they apply a function to multiple variables at once. They differ in that the function aggregates the results to return a single logical vector. 5.1.7 dplyr::pick()
Sometimes we may want to perform a function using several columns simultaneously - for instance, for a mental health measure, to sum the values across several columns into a total Likert score. Base R contains several functions for carrying out row-wise operations, including pmin(), pmax(), rowSums() and rowMeans(), but these functions are not pipe-friendly as, although they use data.frames or tibbles as inputs, they operate on every column (which may include more columns than one wants) and output a single vector, rather than a transformed tibble. pick() instead allows one to specify the correct columns to put into these functions and place them within a pipe. In essence, pick() takes the current tibble and temporarily creates another which has just the columns specified. tidyselect helpers can be used to specify columns.1

5.1.8 Task II

Open the Age 55y NCDS main interview file (ncds_2013_flatfile.dta). Create a CASP-6 Quality of Life score, where higher values indicate better quality of life. To construct this score take the mean item response and set to the score to missing if the cohort member has four or more items missing (hint: rowSums(is.na(df) calculate the number of missing values in a row). Be aware of how each item is coded when answering this question.



Reveal the solution
ncds_55y <- glue("{ncds_fld}/55y/ncds_2013_flatfile.dta") %>% 
  read_dta()

lookfor(ncds_55y, "casp")

ncds_55y %>%
  mutate(across(matches("N9CASP"), negative_to_na)) %>%
  lookfor("casp")

ncds_55y %>%
  select(matches("N9CASP")) %>%
  mutate(across(matches("N9CASP"), negative_to_na),
         across(matches("N9CASP[4-6])"), ~ 5 - .x),
         casp6_mean = rowMeans(pick(matches("N9CASP[1-6]")), na.rm = TRUE), 
         casp6_missing = rowSums(is.na(pick(matches("N9CASP[1-6]")))),
         casp6_mean = ifelse(casp6_missing >= 4, NA, casp6_mean)) %>%
  group_by(casp6_missing) %>%
  slice(1) %>%
  ungroup()

Sweep 6 (14y) of the MCS included several cognitive assessments, including a 20-item vocabularly test. Answers to the individual items are contained in the variables FCCMCOGA to FCCMCOGT within the mcs6_cm_cognitive_assessment.dta file. The value label indicates which answer is correct. Load the data and create a variable for a cohort member’s total score on the test as the number of correct items. Only give a score to an individual if they attempt one or more items.



Reveal the solution
mcs_14y_cog <- glue("{mcs_fld}/14y/mcs6_cm_cognitive_assessment.dta") %>%
  read_dta()

lookfor(mcs_14y_cog)
lookfor(mcs_14y_cog, "FCCMCOG[A-T]")

val_labels(mcs_14y_cog$FCCMCOGA)
val_labels(mcs_14y_cog$FCCMCOGT)

clean_vocab_item <- function(item){
  value_labels <- val_labels(item)
  correct_answer <- value_labels[str_detect(names(value_labels), "\\(correct answer\\)")]
  
  case_when(item == correct_answer ~ 1,
            item %in% 1:5 ~ 0)
}

mcs_14y_cog %>%
  select(MCSID, FCNUM00, matches("FCCMCOG[A-T]")) %>%
  mutate(across(matches("FCCMCOG[A-T]"), clean_vocab_item),
         cog_score = pick(matches("FCCMCOG[A-T]")) %>% rowSums(na.rm = TRUE),
         cog_obs = pick(matches("FCCMCOG[A-T]")) %>% rowSums(!is.na(.)),
         cog_score = ifelse(cog_obs >= 1, cog_score, NA)) %>%
  select(MCSID, FCNUM00, cog_score)

5.2 Writing Functions to Clean Data
As has been discussed, cleaning data is often a repetitive process in LDA: we may need to clean the same variables in the same way across different sweeps. In this case, to make our code efficient and less error-prone, we can write bespoke functions. Below is a function that cleans height and weight data and derives BMI in each of sweeps 3-7 in the MCS. As we saw in Chapter 4, height and weight are contained in the variables XCHTCM00 and XCWTCM00 in each of these sweeps (or XCHTCMA0 and XCWTCMA0 for Sweep 5). This makes the cleaning predictable.

mcs_fups <- c(0, 3, 5, 7, 11, 14, 17)

clean_bmi <- function(sweep){
  sweep_letter <- letters[sweep]
  fup <- mcs_fups[sweep]
  glue("{mcs_fld}/{fup}y/mcs{sweep}_cm_interview.dta") %>%
    read_dta(col_select = c("MCSID",
                            matches("^.(CNUM|C(W|H)TCM)(A|0)0"))) %>%
    rename(cnum = matches(".CNUM00"),
           height_raw = matches(".CHTCM(A|0)0"),
           weight_raw = matches(".CWTCM(A|0)0")) %>%
    mutate(height = negative_to_na(height_raw) %>%
             as.numeric(),
           weight = negative_to_na(weight_raw) %>%
             as.numeric(),
           bmi = weight / ( (height / 100) ^ 2),
           fup = !!fup) %>%
    select(MCSID, cnum, fup, height, weight)
}

5.3 Combining tibbles
A key step in LDA is combining different datasets together - e.g., from different sweeps. This can be done by merging (placing the data in wide format) or by appending (placing the data in long format). We will start by discussing merging and then move on to appending.
To make the process easier to understand, we will use small datasets from sweeps 6 & 7, containing data on height ((F|G)CHTCM00) and weight ((F|G)CWTCM00) from three cohort members (MCSIDs: M10020R, M10025W, and M10002P) who appeared in sweeps 6 only, 7 only, and both sweeps, respectively. Later, to show how to combine more than two datasets at once, we will add in data from the same individuals from Sweep 5, which they all appeared in.

load_mcs_mini <- function(sweep){
  sweep_letter <- letters[sweep]
  fup <- mcs_fups[sweep]
  
  glue("{mcs_fld}/{fup}y/mcs{sweep}_cm_interview.dta") %>%
    read_dta(col_select = c("MCSID", matches("^.(CNUM|C(W|H)TCM)(A|0)0"))) %>%
    filter(MCSID %in% c("M10020R", "M10025W", "M10002P")) %>%
    arrange(MCSID)
}

5.3.1 Merging tibbles with dplyr::*_join()
To merge two tibbles together - i.e., to create a new tibble with columns from both tibbles - we can use the dplyr mutating *_join() functions. These are called mutating joins because they add new columns to the outputted tibble. The functions differ in the rows that each retain in the output tibble.

full_join(x, y, by = ...): Returns all rows from x and y . The missing value NA is used to fill cells that are created during the merge. Rows in x with no match in y will have NA values in the new columns from y. Rows in y with no match in x will have NA values in the columns of x.
inner_join(x, y, by = ...): Returns all rows from x and y where there are matching rows in both tibbles.
left_join(x, y, by = ...): Returns all rows from x Rows in x with no match in y will have NA values in the new columns from y.
right_join(x, y, by = ...): Returns all rows from y, and all columns from x and y. Rows in y with no match in x will have NA values in the columns of x.

To join the two datasets together, we need to specify the columns to join by (the “key” variables). By default, *_join() functions will use all variables with common names across the two datasets as the key variables. To specify particular columns, we can instead provide a character vector of the joining columns to the by argument. Joining columns do not need to have the same name in each tibble. If they have different names, we can specify a named vector. The names of this vector are names of the columns in the left (x) tibble and the values of the vector are the names of the columns in the right (y) tibble. In the merged tibble, key columns retain the names from the left tibble. Let’s see the functions in action:

full_join(mcs_14y_mini,
          mcs_17y_mini,
          by = c("MCSID", FCNUM00 = "GCNUM00"))

More complicated rules for identifying rows to merge than above can be specified with the join_by() helper function. This is unlikely to be needed for most LDA applications, so we do not discuss this further here (an exception you may come across is joining overlapping activity history datasets) - see the dplyr website for more detail.

5.3.1.1 Merging 2+ tibbles with purrr::reduce()
What if we want to merge more than two datasets together - for instance, merge all seven sweeps of the MCS? Writing out each *_join() function separately would be cumbersome. Instead, we can use purrr::reduce() to chain together successive *_join() function calls, aggregating the result.
reduce() is similar to map() in that repeats a function for each object within an input. But unlike map(), the result from an iteration back into the next iteration. Specifically, reduce() takes an object, applies a function, f, to the first two element and then takes the result and inputs it into f along with the next element of the inputted object, repeating this until the object is exhausted. For instance, specifying inner_join() in reduce() with a list of three tibbles will perform inner_join() on the first two, and then perform inner_join() on the result from that with the third tibble.
The syntax for reduce() is similar to map2() where .x and .y refer to the first and second elements of the list, respectively, or to the result and to the next element of the list. Below we perform an inner_join() on data from sweeps 5-7. Note, as the XCNUM00 joining keys differ depending on which sweeps are being merged, we need to slightly alter the code used above to account for this.2

     mcs_17y_mini) %>%
  reduce(
    ~ inner_join(
      .x %>% rename(CNUM = matches("CNUM")),
      .y %>% rename(CNUM = matches("CNUM")) ,
      by = c("MCSID", "CNUM")
    )
  )

5.3.1.2 Filtering Joins
dplyr also contains two filtering join functions, semi_join(x, y) and anti_join(x, y). Unlike mutating joins, these do not add new columns to the outputted tibble. Instead, they filter rows in x depending on whether there is a match in y or not.

semi_join(x, y, by = ...): Returns all rows from x that have matches in y. Keeps columns just from x.
anti_join(x, y, by = ...): Returns all rows from x that do not have matches in y. Keeps columns just from x.

We have seen how the mutating *_join() functions can be used to merge tibbles together in wide format. Appending data with bind_rows() allows us to place data in long format. bind_rows() is simple - it takes a set of tibbles and then stacks these in the order they are specified. If the inputs are named, the .id argument can be used to populate a column in the outputted tibble identifying the input tibble a given row came from.
